forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Dorset Council's risk register rates schools high needs funding instability "High", unchanged since Quarter 4
news_drafts.lead:
Dorset Council's Audit and Governance Committee, meeting on 12 October 2026, has before it a risk register entry rating as "High" the possibility that instability in the high needs budget could push the council into deficit. High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The rating is unchanged from Quarter 4.

The entry, numbered Risk 194, says that "Instability in the High Needs Block budget may create an increased deficit in the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) resulting in a deficit in Dorset Councils financial position." The dedicated schools grant is the government grant that funds schools. A deficit on it would be an overspend, usually on support for children with special needs. The papers give no figures for the size of the deficit or the budget.

The same issue appears in the committee's action list. A previous report identified the instability as a significant matter and asked for reassurance from the Cabinet Member for Education and Finance. The action is recorded as in progress, with no completion date. The tracker says the instability "may create increased deficit in the dedicated school grant resulting in deficit in Dorset Council's financial position".

news_drafts.headline: Dorset Council forecasts £73.7m schools overspend, taking cumulative deficit to £221.9m
news_drafts.lead:
Dorset Council expects to overspend its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) by £73.737m in 2026-27, according to papers for its Schools' Forum on 25 September. That would lift the cumulative deficit from £148.7m at 31 March 2026 to £221.87m. The forecast is as at 31 July, and the overspend sits in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities.

In-year overspends were £23.7m in 2023-24 and £37.3m in 2024-25. The deficit stood at £35.9m in April 2023. Over that period the council received £23.75m from the Department for Education and contributed £3.9m through schools block transfers. The papers name the continued rise in Education, Health and Care Plans since the 2014 reforms as a significant driver. Current plan numbers are unavailable because of reporting delays since the Synergy case management system began on 7 May 2025.

The deficit is kept off the council's main balance sheet under a statutory override (a temporary government rule), extended to March 2028. The council still has £148.7m less cash than it otherwise would, which costs £4.9m a year in interest foregone, met from its General Fund. Government says support in 2026/27 and 2027/28 will be "appropriate and proportionate" and "will not be unlimited". Dorset submitted its Local SEND Reform Plans in June 2026, with outcomes expected in autumn 2026.

findings.headline: Early Years Block and Funding audit issued limited assurance opinion with four improvement actions
findings.detail: The audit of Early Years Block and Funding (2026/27) resulted in a limited assurance opinion, indicating significant control deficiencies. Four improvement actions are required, comprising three medium-risk actions and one low-risk action, overall rated as medium risk.
findings.matters: Early years services are statutory and grant-funded; limited assurance indicates control or compliance issues in how grant funding is managed, allocated, and reported.
findings.figures: 4 actions required: 0 major, 3 medium risk, 1 low risk; overall risk rating: Medium
findings.quote: Assurance Early Years Block and Funding 2 Final Limited 4 - 3 1 Medium

findings.headline: Fleet Maintenance audit issued limited assurance opinion with five improvement actions
findings.detail: The audit of Fleet Maintenance (2025/26) resulted in a limited assurance opinion, indicating significant control deficiencies. Five improvement actions are required, comprising one major action, three medium-risk actions, and one low-risk action, overall rated as medium risk.
findings.matters: Fleet is a material operating cost for councils; limited assurance on fleet maintenance controls indicates control weaknesses in asset management, cost control, and value for money in a significant area of spending.
findings.figures: 5 actions required: 1 major, 3 medium risk, 1 low risk; overall risk rating: Medium
findings.quote: Assurance Fleet Maintenance – 25/26 Final Limited 5 1 3 1 Medium

findings.headline: 30 audit actions overdue, including six to twelve months late
findings.detail: Of 61 audit actions arising from previous audits that have yet to be implemented, 30 are currently overdue. The report notes that 20% of the overdue actions have been overdue for between six and twelve months. The council has stopped revising implementation dates to avoid masking the scale of delay.
findings.matters: Overdue audit actions indicate the council is not implementing control improvements within a reasonable timeframe, which is a governance concern for lenders and external oversight bodies assessing council risk.
findings.figures: 30 overdue actions out of 61 total actions not yet implemented; 20% of overdue actions are six to twelve months late
findings.quote: There are 61 actions that have yet to be implemented, 30 of which are currently overdue. 20% of the overdue actions are between 6 and 12 months overdue.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered £21m below budget, reducing financing requirement and lowering external borrowing below plan
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement of £449m at year-end was £21m below the budget of £470m approved in February 2025, due to slippage in the capital programme. External borrowing increased by £23m during the year, £10m less than budgeted, reflecting the lower planned capital spend. Interest payable consequently came in at £11.9m against a budget of £14.2m, a favorable variance of £2.3m.
findings.matters: Programme delays affect both the council's financing requirements and the timing of planned infrastructure delivery; persistent slippage may signal capacity issues or funding constraints that could defer service improvements.
findings.figures: CFR £449m actual versus £470m budget (£21m underspend); external borrowing +£23m actual versus approximately £33m budgeted; interest payable £11.9m actual versus £14.2m budget
findings.quote: The Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) at 31 March 2026 was £449m, up £15m from £434m at the start of the year but £21m below the budget of £470m when the capital strategy was approved by full Council in February 2025

findings.headline: Cash and treasury investments reduced from £58m to £25m as council divested from pooled funds to manage borrowing position
findings.detail: The council's cash and treasury investments fell by £33m (57%) during 2025-26, from £58m to £25m. This was a deliberate strategy to offset external borrowing requirements by divesting from inherited pooled fund portfolios. The investment portfolio declined from £27.7m to £1.3m, and investment income fell to £4.9m from a budget of £6.9m as a result of both the smaller portfolio and reduced yields from interest rate cuts during the year.
findings.matters: This material reduction in liquid reserves significantly affects the council's financial flexibility and internal borrowing capacity, signalling a structural shift toward reliance on external debt and potentially constraining the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or fund future capital investment.
findings.figures: Cash and investments £25m at 31 March 2026 versus £58m at 31 March 2025; investment holdings down from £27.7m to £1.3m; investment income £4.9m actual versus £6.9m budget
findings.quote: Cash and cash equivalents of £24m and treasury investments valued at £1m, in total £25m, down £33m from £58m at 31 March 2025
